title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F01
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 45 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)
EO science strategy and scientific literature

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

items.question: Download two Sentinel-2 true-colour images with maximum cloud cover of 20% covering Los Angeles County, California, USA — one acquired in the period December 2024–7 January 2025 and one acquired in the period 31 January–28 February 2025 — to assess landscape changes caused by the Palisades and Eaton wildfires. Compare the two images and determine whether visible changes such as burn scars, vegetation loss, reduced vegetation greenness, smoke impacts, and other landscape changes are observable between the early- and post-fire periods.

answers.text:
After loading and comparing the two Sentinel-2 true-colour images of Los Angeles County, California, acquired during the specified periods (December 2024–January 2025 and January–February 2025), the following observations can be made regarding landscape changes caused by the Palisades and Eaton wildfires:

1. Burn Scars and Vegetation Loss:
   • The image from January–February 2025 shows more pronounced areas of brownish discoloration compared to the December 2024–January 2025 image. These areas correspond to the locations of the Palisades and Eaton wildfires, indicating significant vegetation loss and burn scars.
   • The burned areas appear as darker, more uniform patches, contrasting with the surrounding green and brown vegetation.

2. Reduced Vegetation Greenness:
   • The vegetation in the affected areas appears less vibrant and greener in the January–February 2025 image, suggesting a reduction in vegetation greenness due to the fire's impact.
   • The contrast between the burned areas and the surrounding vegetation is more evident in the later image, highlighting the extent of the damage.

3. Smoke Impacts:
   • There is no visible evidence of smoke impacts in either image, as the images were acquired under clear conditions with ≤20% cloud cover. The absence of smoke suggests that the smoke had dissipated by the time of the second image acquisition.

4. Other Landscape Changes:
   • The urban areas and infrastructure remain largely unchanged between the two images, indicating that the fire's impact was primarily confined to the natural vegetation and surrounding areas.
   • The coastal areas and water bodies appear unaffected, as expected, given their distance from the fire-affected regions.

In conclusion, the comparison of the two images clearly demonstrates the visible changes caused by the Palisades and Eaton wildfires, including burn scars, vegetation loss, and reduced vegetation greenness. The absence of smoke impacts suggests that the fire's effects were primarily localized to the affected areas. Here is the full content of the EO Dashboard narrative on forest cover loss, titled "Forests on the Brink: Satellite Imagery unveiling Loss and Shifting Forest Landscapes":

Frontmatter (Metadata)
• Cover Image: Forest Hero Image (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eurodatacube/eodash-assets/main/stories/forest_story/hero.jpg)
• Date: 2025-01-01
• Theme: Biomass
• Tags: forest
• Official Narrative: Yes
• STAC Collections Used:
  • FNF_Palsar (Forest/Non-Forest classification)
  • E10e_ndvi (Vegetation indices)
  • LIS_Global_DA_Evap (Evapotranspiration)
  • RECCAP2_6_deforested_biomass (Deforested biomass)
  • N2_CO2_diff (CO₂ differences)
  • RECCAP2_5_SF_biomass_growth (Sustainable forest biomass growth)

Narrative Summary
Introduction
This collaborative narrative by ESA, NASA, and JAXA underscores the role of satellites in tracking forest loss and degradation. Forests, covering 31% of global land, are critical for biodiversity and carbon storage but face threats from deforestation, climate change, and fires. Annual losses of 10 million hectares (2015–2020) contribute to 15% of global carbon emissions.

Key Insights
1. Global Forest Crisis:
   • Deforestation and degradation risk irreversible tipping points, disrupting ecosystems and local climates.
   • The UN FAO reports persistent forest loss despite a slowing trend.

2. Satellite Monitoring:
   • The Glasgow Leaders’ Declaration (COP26) aims to halt deforestation by 2030, with satellites providing real-time data for accountability.
   • Multi-sensor approaches (optical, radar) are essential for accurate monitoring.

3. Data-Driven Analysis:
   • Six STAC collections are used to analyze:
     • Forest cover changes (FNF_Palsar).
     • Biomass loss (RECCAP2_6_deforested_biomass).
     • CO₂ impacts (N2_CO2_diff).
     • Vegetation health (E10e_ndvi).

4. Call to Action:
   • Satellites enable transparent tracking of global commitments to protect forests.

Full Text Access
For the complete narrative (including visuals and detailed analysis), visit:
 EO Dashboard: Forest Loss and Degradation (https://ESA-eodashboards.github.io/eodashboard-narratives/forest_loss_and_degradation.md)

Next Steps:
• Explore the STAC collections (e.g., FNF_Palsar for forest cover data).
• Search for related narratives on deforestation or biomass.
• Retrieve sample data from the referenced collections.

items.question: Search EO Dashboard narratives related to sea surface temperature patterns. Identify a representative coastal location discussed in a narrative, retrieve ERA5 monthly mean sea surface temperature within a 2° × 2° region around that location for three representative years from different decades, and compute the multi-year mean SST field to characterize typical ocean temperature conditions.

answers.text:
The multi-year mean sea surface temperature (SST) field for the 2° × 2° region around 8°S, 80°W (near the coast of Peru) has been successfully computed. Here is the final output:

Output File
• File Path: mean_sst_1990_2000_2010_peru_coast.nc

Steps to Generate the File (Recap)
1. Convert SST from Kelvin to Celsius for all three years (1990, 2000, 2010).
2. Clip the data to the bounding box:
   • North: -6.0°
   • South: -10.0°
   • East: -79.0°
   • West: -81.0°
3. Compute the multi-year mean SST for the three years combined.
4. Save the result as a NetCDF file.

How to Use the File
You can open and visualize the file using tools like:
• Python (xarray, matplotlib, cartopy)
• QGIS (for spatial analysis)
• Panoply (for quick visualization)

For example, in Python:

import xarray as xr
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Load the file
ds = xr.open_dataset("mean_sst_1990_2000_2010_peru_coast.nc")

Plot the mean SST
ds["sst"].plot()
plt.title("Multi-Year Mean SST (1990, 2000, 2010) - Coastal Peru")
plt.show()

Here are the science questions from the ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy (EOSS) knowledge base that are related to land surface temperature monitoring:

Key Science Questions
1. [SQ-43] What are the main coupling determinants between Earth's energy, water, and carbon cycles?
   • Relevance: Focuses on quantifying relationships between energy fluxes (including land surface temperature), water, and carbon cycles, and their influence on climate feedbacks.
   • Key Objectives:
     • Quantify land-atmosphere interactions across spatio-temporal scales.
     • Study surface and upper-atmosphere forcings in boundary layer processes.

2. [SQ-46] How does the Earth's energy imbalance and Earth heat inventory change over time and why?
   • Relevance: Directly tied to monitoring surface temperature as part of the Earth's energy budget and heat distribution.
   • Key Objectives:
     • Evaluate the Earth's heat inventory.
     • Close the global energy budget.
     • Study temporal changes in the Earth's energy imbalance.

3. [SQ-48] How can we improve the monitoring and understanding of planetary heat exchange at regional scales?
   • Relevance: Explicitly targets improving regional-scale monitoring of heat exchange, including land surface temperature.
   • Key Objectives:
     • Improve understanding of thermal air-surface feedback mechanisms.
     • Advance knowledge of extreme events (e.g., heatwaves).
     • Study momentum and kinetic energy transfer in the Earth system.

4. [SQ-56] Where and how are ecosystems undergoing critical transitions?
   • Relevance: Land surface temperature is a key indicator of ecosystem health and resilience, driving critical transitions.
   • Key Objectives:
     • Assess ecosystem dynamics, including disturbance frequency and recovery rates.
     • Understand links between vegetation characteristics and climate.

5. [SQ-45] How can we reduce uncertainties in climate sensitivity while improving estimates of internal energy flow within the climate system?
   • Relevance: Addresses climate sensitivity, which is influenced by surface temperature and energy fluxes.
   • Key Objectives:
     • Reduce uncertainties in regional energy fluxes.
     • Study cumulative regional cloud feedbacks.

6. [SQ-10] How do extreme events (e.g., heatwaves, droughts) impact ecosystems and societies?
   • Relevance: Focuses on the impacts of extreme events like heatwaves, which are directly tied to land surface temperature monitoring.

These questions highlight the importance of land surface temperature in understanding energy fluxes, ecosystem health, climate sensitivity, and extreme events.
